newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA URGES EQUAL START ON EUROPEAN INTEGRATION TALKS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA URGES EQUAL START ON EUROPEAN INTEGRATION TALKS.

text.p: Bulgaria said on Monday that all former communist countries should start negotiations for European Union entry at the same time after the EU left the reform laggard state out of its first wave of expansion.

"A decision of the European Union for an equal start of negotiations with all applicants would be a confirmation that all countries have equal chances to become members of United Europe," said a government's declaration.
"The conditions and the time for finalising the negotiations, of course, will be different depending on the stage of readiness of each country," the declaration said.

The European Commission invited Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Estonia and Slovenia for EU entry talks last week presenting its Agenda 2000 policy document mapping out plans to expand beyond the former Iron Curtain early next century.

The EU rejected Bulgaria, Romania, Lithuania, Latvia and Slovakia pledging to design a pre-accession strategy which will help them act on their shortcomings and prepare for the obligations of full membership. The Commission will review the progress of each of these applicants each year.
Bulgaria's government said the country had fallen far behind other East European states in implementing market economy principles, land reform, privatisation and development of the private sector.
"This set back is a result of an accumulated inactivity and wrong government decisions in recent years," the declaration said.
Bulgaria appreciates the stand of the European Commission that the new reformist government has clearly showed that it will set in train rapid reforms, it said.

The government of the Union of Democratic Forces took office on May 21 after the government of the Bulgarian Socialist Party was ousted from power in February by mass protests and early elections were held in mid-April.

The Commission has said Bulgaria was on its way to satisfying the political criteria for EU membership, but its economic progress had been limited by the absence of a commitment to market-oriented policies.

This policy should permit recovery from the crisis of recent months which saw a negative growth (- 10.9 percent of GDP in 1996), worsening public deficits, hyper-inflation (311 percent in 1996) and depreciation of the currency.

Foreign Minister Nadejda Mihailova said last week that winning social support for reforms, the government was optimistic that Bulgaria would soon overcome its economic problems and compensate reform delays, which impeded its way to the EU.
